short: Armigeri (latin) translates as «armored, equipped for war», but has a much broader meaning. The word itself comes from «arma» (military equipment) + «gerere» (to carry) and literally translates as Armadillos or much more understandable meaning Squires, but to compare them, exactly with medieval squires, is not worth it at all, as even in the times of late medieval England this word referred not to a simple squire accompanying the knight, and special - carrying his unique emblem. Armigeri, probably should be meant as «armored» or even «heavily armored». Many researchers believe that cavalry units Armigeri were some equivalent of mounted cataphracts, but the question remains as to what were similarly named infantry units. It is quite possible that the soldiers of these legions were particularly well protected or armed; another explanation may be that they earned this nickname or insignia by demonstrating their fortitude. The word Armaturarum has a very similar meaning to Armigeri.
history: In the face of an increasing number of barbarian incursions, the effective defence of Rome’s now-sprawling territory became a serious problem in the 4th century AD. The Emperor Constantine’s controversial solution was to divide the army into two halves. 'Limitanei', literally ‘the men on the limes’ or 'borders', were frontier garrison troops intended to pin down an invading force until the full-time 'comitatenses', the late-Roman equivalent of the traditional Legionaries, could arrive to deal with the situation decisively. Although well-equipped, limitanei were generally considered by all to be second-class warriors. This was possibly because they were often part-time soldiers who had been encouraged to settle and farm the land around their outposts in exchange for policing the Empire's borders.
strengths: Very low damage and armour penetration
